Also referred to as a "trayning field," over 1000 Redcoats made camp on the Common during the British occupation of Boston in 1775. You are here Home › Cemeteries › Granary Burying Ground Last updated: 2/20/26 Granary Burying Ground The Granary Burying Ground, located at 120 Tremont Street in downtown Boston, is the city's third oldest cemetery. The Granary Burying Ground was the third burial site in Boston Proper, established in 1660. Town officials set aside part of what was then the Boston Common for burial space to help alleviate overcrowding in the near-by King’s Chapel Burying Ground. First, the space was known as the South or Common Burying Ground, and then the Middle Burying Ground (after the opening of Central Burying Ground). The Granary Burying Ground took its present name in 1737 when a granary, a small building used to store grain, was moved to the site presently occupied by the Park Street Church. The Granary Burying Grounds contains approximately 2,345 gravestones and tombs, although it is estimated that over 5,000 people are buried at this site. The grave markers are predominantly slate. The gravestones’ original configuration was rearranged into straighter rows over the years to accommodate both nineteenth-century aesthetics and the modern lawnmower. Underground burial crypts (tombs) line the entire perimeter of the site. These crypts are small rectangular rooms, made of brick or stone, designed to hold multiple burials, which were frequently owned by families. Older underground tombs are found in the center of the site. Many well-known people from American history are buried at this site. Go to Shop The History of 263 Summer St A Building That Helped Shape the City Long before it became home, 263 Summer Street played a working role in Boston’s industrial rise. Constructed in 1905 by the Boston Wharf Company, the building was part of a network of warehouses, offices, and manufacturing spaces that defined Fort Point as one of the city’s most productive districts. Designed by architect Morton D. Safford , whose work helped shape the neighborhood, the building was created for durability, efficiency, and longevity—qualities that still define it today. From the start, this was a place built to last. Summer Street & “Wool Row” At the turn of the 20th century, Summer Street was known as “Wool Row” —the customer-facing edge of Boston’s wool and textile trade. Merchants, manufacturers, and logistics operations lined the corridor, connecting industry to the waterfront, the rail system, and the rest of the city. Early tenants reflected that energy and scale, including the U.S. Army Depot Quartermaster , Windrum Shoe Manufacturing , and the Boston Wool Trade Association . This building wasn’t ornamental—it was essential. Built on Resilience The story goes deeper than the brick walls. Fort Point itself was built on land created from the debris of Boston’s Great Fire of 1872 —a city-scale reset that led to a stronger, more modern Boston. That cycle of reinvention is literally beneath your feet, embedded in the character of the district, and carried forward by the buildings that rose from it. The Sign That Never Went Dark Rising above Summer Street is the iconic red neon “Boston Wharf Co Industrial Real Estate” sign—a fixture that has guided pedestrians and commuters for generations. Officially recognized within Fort Point’s landmark guidelines, the sign has been described as a beacon marking the passage from downtown into Boston’s industrial age. Over the years, it has been repainted and reinterpreted by local artists, reinforcing its role as more than signage—it’s a cultural marker. While much around it has changed, the sign remains, anchoring the building to its origins. A New Chapter Begins More than a century after its construction, 263 Summer Street enters its next era as part of Boston’s office-to-housing transformation—preserving what makes the building significant while reimagining what it can be. The exterior remains unmistakably historic. Inside, the spaces have been fully modernized for contemporary living, with clean lines, warm materials, and thoughtful layouts that respect the building’s industrial bones without replicating the past. This isn’t history frozen in time—it’s history, adapted. Still Standing. Still Evolving. Today, 263 Summer Street stands as a rare balance: a building with memory, character, and presence—redefined for the way Boston lives now. What began as a place of work has become a place to live. The large-scale redevelopment of Boston’s Seaport district is part of a $22 billion dollar attempt to turn a working waterfront into a mixed-use urban neighborhood.
